title: Cache-Conscious Programming
summary: Writing code that respects the memory hierarchy — where mechanical sympathy turns into measurable speedups.

slides.subTitle: Coding with the hierarchy in mind
slides.markdown:
**Mechanical sympathy** means writing code with an awareness of how the hardware underneath actually behaves — specifically, that memory access is cheap when it respects locality and expensive when it doesn't, regardless of what the algorithm's asymptotic complexity says.

Two pieces of code with identical Big-O can differ by 5-10x in wall-clock time purely from how well they use the cache. This topic covers the concrete techniques for writing the faster version deliberately, not by luck.

slides.subTitle: Shrink the working set on purpose
slides.markdown:
**Tiling** (or **blocking**) restructures nested loops to process a small **tile** of the data at a time — small enough that the tile fits entirely in a fast cache level — instead of sweeping the whole array in one pass.

The win: every element in a tile gets reused several times while it's still cache-resident, instead of being evicted before its next use. This is the single most important cache-conscious technique for anything with nested loops over large arrays — matrix multiply, image processing, numerical simulation.

slides.subTitle: Blocked vs naive matrix multiply
Array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays
slides.markdown:
**Array-of-structs (AoS)** stores `{x, y, z}` objects one after another — natural to read, but if you only need `x` from every object, each cache line wastes space on `y` and `z` you didn't want. **Struct-of-arrays (SoA)** stores all `x` values contiguously, then all `y`, then all `z` — a scan over just `x` uses every byte of every fetched cache line.

Neither layout is universally better: AoS wins when you process whole objects together; SoA wins when you scan one field across many objects — exactly the access pattern in most data-parallel and SIMD code.

slides.subTitle: Independent data, same line
slides.markdown:
**False sharing** happens when two threads update *logically independent* variables that happen to sit on the **same cache line**. Coherence protocols work per-line, not per-variable, so each thread's write invalidates the other's copy of the whole line — even though neither thread ever touches the other's data.

The result looks like true contention (constant cache-to-cache traffic and stalls) but the fix has nothing to do with locking — it's purely about layout: padding or separating the variables onto different cache lines (cross-link: multicore).

slides.subTitle: Two counters, one line
Big-O isn't the whole story
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Two algorithms with the same Big-O complexity run at roughly the same real speed."

**Why it's wrong:** Big-O hides the **constant factor**, and cache behavior is one of its largest contributors. A naive and a cache-blocked O(N^3) matrix multiply do the same arithmetic, yet the blocked version can run several times faster by keeping data in cache longer.

**Correct model:** Big-O describes scaling, not wall-clock time at a given size. For performance-critical code, access pattern is often the dominant real cost — invisible to asymptotic analysis.

slides.subTitle: Linked lists vs arrays
slides.markdown:
Traversing a linked list means following a pointer to wherever its node happens to live in memory — allocations scattered across the heap have no relationship to each other, so each `node->next` is likely a fresh cache miss with nothing to prefetch, since the hardware can't know an address until it dereferences the previous one.

An array traversal, by contrast, is fully predictable: element `i+1` sits right after element `i`, so the hardware prefetcher can stream ahead and hide the latency almost entirely. This is why a `std::vector`-of-values scan can be several times faster than an equivalent linked-list walk with the same element count, even though both are O(n) — the difference is entirely in whether the next address is knowable in advance.
